text.p: Exploratory work on the Escondida Norte copper deposit has yielded encouraging results but details on how and when it will be developed are a long way off, Broken Hill Pty chairman Jerry Ellis said.
The deposit, a few km north of the Escondida open pit mine, looks very attractive after exploratory drilling, Ellis told a news conference in Santiago.
"We're drilling at the moment and increasing our knowledge of the shape, grade and size of the ore body. It looks very attractive," he said.

Made up mainly of sulphides but with some oxides, the deposit straddles the property line between Escondida, majority owned by BHP, and the Zaldivar copper mine owned by Finland's Outokumpu Oy and Canada's Placer Dome.

Escondida officials have declined to give estimates on the size of Escondida Norte, except to say that it's smaller than the main Escondida ore body and that they don't consider it now a priority for development.
He said Escondida, Chile's second largest mining company after state-owned Codelco, was busily exploring for new copper and gold deposits throughout Chile and neighboring countries.

"We have a very active and quite large exploration team based in Santiago. They are looking for copper, gold and other metals...in Chile, Argentina and Peru. We believe Chile to be highly prospective and we'd be delighted if we found another Escondida," said Ellis, leading an Australian trade delegation.

He said that although the Bajo de la Alumbrera copper mine in Argentina was using existing railroads to carry concentrates to Atlantic ports, future mines in Argentina might look at other ways to bring concentrates over the Andes to Chilean ports.
One possibility would be to build a slurry pipeline to carry concentrates mixed with water, like the pipeline Escondida uses to send concentrates to port, he said.
"But that's wild and visionary speculation. The practical solution for now is to ship concentrates to the Atlantic," he said, including for BHP's Agua Rica mine in northern Argentina.
